prize_parts.citation: For developing empirical methods to estimate demand for differentiated products and the dynamics of competition in industries.

statement.case_for: Random-coefficients demand estimation with endogenous prices (Berry 1994; Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes 1995), together with Pakes's dynamic-industry and estimation work, is both a method and a framework. It lets researchers recover substitution patterns, market power and welfare from market data. That is the combination I value: a new tool plus a structure that gives it economic meaning, as with data discovery paired with an explanatory framework. Its reach is well beyond one subfield. It is the working toolkit for merger review and antitrust, and it is used in empirical trade, health, environmental and productivity work. The core papers are about thirty years old, so adoption, replication, software and identification critiques are all mature. Colleagues who ranked the other leading candidates highly did not point to an earlier prize directly covering this ground. Attribution to the three BLP authors is compact and identifiable. I have not changed my first-place view after reading the openings. I do regard B002 as a very close and defensible alternative.
statement.case_against: The three-name limit leaves out Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin. Bresnahan's work on identifying market power and product differentiation is arguably foundational to the empirical IO programme, so the trio may look incomplete. The prize would reward a toolkit more than a single substantive finding. Results depend on structural assumptions, and identification and computational critiques remain active. It is also unclear whether the Committee would classify this as industrial organisation or as econometrics, which could affect how its breadth is judged.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B012 first and treats Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes as the clear centre of demand estimation, while noting that a three-name award omits real contributors such as Bresnahan and Reiss.
responses.response: I agree on the BLP core and on the breadth of use in regulatory and merger practice. I am less sure than he is that the omissions are a minor cost. If Bresnahan's earlier contributions on market power and differentiation were judged equal in kind to the demand-estimation breakthrough, no three-person set around BLP would be fully defensible. For now I read the discovery as the demand-side inversion plus Pakes's dynamic framework, which supports the trio. I would want the citation worded narrowly enough that it does not imply credit for all of empirical IO.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B002 first and adds Gertler to Kiyotaki and Moore for the financial-accelerator strand. He acknowledges that Bernanke's 2022 prize limits room for that strand and says the credit division is contestable.
responses.response: I agree that Kiyotaki-Moore is a foundational mechanism and that its maturity is not in doubt. I would resist adding Gertler. The accelerator lineage runs through Bernanke, who is already recognised, and a blended citation would invite the attribution dispute Hassler himself flags. The clean version is Kiyotaki and Moore for collateral-driven amplification. That is a strong alternative to my preference. The empirical identification of the collateral channel is less clean than the theory, which several colleagues note and which I weigh against it. I therefore keep B012 first while naming B002 as my main fallback.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B025 first and B002 second, calls Kiyotaki-Moore a clean two-author attribution, and ranks B012 third while saying he should discount any personal affinity with the subfield.
responses.response: I accept the point about B002's clean attribution, and it is the main reason B002 is my first alternative. I read the B012 methodological case differently from the way his discount suggests. The case rests on how much downstream research and policy practice depends on the method, not on subfield closeness. I share his caution about Bresnahan and the long credited list, and I handle it by keeping the award to the BLP and dynamic-estimation core. On B025, I find the Melitz selection model compelling and mature. I rank it below B012 mainly because of overlap with the 2008 new trade theory prize and the uncertain credit to related contributors outside the credited list, such as Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B012 fourth. He accepts the BLP credit but worries that the Committee would have to justify the three-name limit and that there is debate over methodological tools versus substantive discovery.
responses.response: The tool-versus-discovery concern is fair, and it is the strongest general objection to my preference. My answer is that the contribution is a measurement framework with identifiable economic content. It recovers demand elasticities, markups and welfare effects that changed what regulators and researchers can credibly conclude. It is not only a statistical device. I do not think that fully settles the question, and a Committee that places conceptual discovery above measurement would reasonably favour B002 or B025. Where I disagree is on the limit of three. I treat it as a constraint on the citation, not as evidence against the discovery.

uncertainties: Whether Bresnahan's contributions on market power and product differentiation should share credit, or whether Pakes alone, or Pakes with Berry, is the more defensible set.
Whether the Committee treats structural estimation as a substantive discovery or as a methodological toolkit, and how it weighs the two.
Whether B002 (Kiyotaki and Moore) should replace B012 as my first choice. I judge its attribution cleaner but its empirical identification weaker, and that trade-off is not resolved.
Whether the 2022 prize (Bernanke) and the 2008 prize (Krugman) create overlap that the Committee would weigh against B002 and B025.
I cannot independently verify citation counts or adoption figures, or relative credit within the structural-IO group, from the supplied evidence.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My research is in labour economics and the economics of crime, and my frequent co-authors (Bayer, Anwar, Lindquist, Holmlund, Lochner, Bindler) are not among the credited names on any shortlisted ballot.
